scope: A work of political and social analysis with no narrative cast of its own -- every entity is category Reference, per editorial policy's treatise guidance. As the automation queue's own note anticipated ("Named Americans and Europeans; watch place-versus-person"), this book names a large and varied real cast -- American founders and Presidents, legal commentators, colonial historians, geographers and travelers on Native American subjects, and a wide scatter of European philosophers and men of letters cited singly across Volume II's many short chapters -- but remains reference-light relative to its size (2258 paragraphs, ~1547 distinct capitalized word forms in a full-book sweep, comparable to The Wealth of Nations's ~1463 despite being somewhat longer). Volume I's long historical and legal chapters, especially the 372-paragraph chapter on the future condition of the three races (Native Americans, whites, and enslaved Africans) and the 238-paragraph Federal Constitution chapter, carry almost the entire named cast; Volume II's 75 short chapters name comparatively few people, mostly single scattered classical or literary citations. Five person-versus-place or namesake checks were made and resolved cleanly from context, without needing the escape hatch: bare "Washington" (the person dominates seven-to-one over the one reference to the city sharing his name, and is bound accordingly, with the minority place-reference documented rather than silently absorbed), Philip of Macedon vs. Metacom ("King Philip"; the two never share a literal name-string in this book), Jacques-Louis David the painter vs. the biblical King David (the biblical king is never separately named here), and two place names that are not people at all -- "Peter"/"Francis" (parts of the St. Peter's and St. Francis rivers) and "Chester" (a New York county). Bare "Caesar" is left unbound throughout, used only as a generic nickname or byword for seizing power, never as a specific narrative reference. Edition divergence in this book is markedly smaller than in Leviathan or The Wealth of Nations: only two spelling variants were found and aliased ("Sylla"/"Sulla", "Sevigne"/"Sévigné"). Both editions were read and reviewed independently.
